chapters.name: Chapter 1: Building a strong farmer group

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Why farmers group together
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: List what a group could do for your farm that you cannot do alone, and the risks to manage.
This lesson builds toward: For your farm and neighbours, you will list what a group could do that one farmer cannot, and the risks to manage, naming at least three benefits and three common reasons groups fail.
The International Cooperative Alliance defines a cooperative as an association of people who join voluntarily to meet shared economic, social and cultural needs through a business they own together and control democratically. Members are both the owners and the users.
Groups help farmers: buy seed, fertilizer and feed in bulk at lower prices; collect produce into lorry loads that big buyers want; bargain for better prices; share stores, dryers, transport and equipment; get training, certification and credit that lenders give more easily to a group with records; and speak with one voice to government and buyers.
Groups also fail. Common reasons are weak trust, leaders who take control, poor records, members selling to side buyers after the group has agreed a deal, and late payment. The rest of this course is about avoiding these. Groups range from informal self-help or producer groups to registered cooperative societies; a group can start informally and register later.
Words to know:
- Cooperative: a business owned and controlled by its members, who also use its services.
- Producer group: farmers growing the same crop who work together, registered or not.
- Bulk buying: buying large amounts together for a lower price.
- Side-selling: a member selling to another buyer after the group has agreed to sell together.
Official sources:
- International Cooperative Alliance: the cooperative identity, values and principles
Try it now: Write three things a group could do for your farm that you cannot do alone, and the one risk you worry about most. Ask two neighbours what they would want from a group and write their answers.
You can now explain what a cooperative is, what a group can do for farmers, and the main reasons groups fail.

check.q: Which kinds of farmer groups exist?
options: From informal self-help or producer groups to registered cooperative societies
Only groups of more than 1,000 farmers
check.why: Groups range from informal self-help or producer groups to registered cooperatives.

check.q: Your neighbours want to sell maize together but are not ready to register. What can they do?
options: Wait until they can register before doing anything
Ask a trader to be their leader
Start as an informal group and register later
check.why: A group can start informally and register later.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Forming the group: by-laws and registration
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Draft the main by-law rules for a group and find out where to register it.
This lesson builds toward: For a new or existing farmer group, you will draft the main by-law rules and name the office where the group would register, with at least five key rules and the current steps checked with the office.
Start with people who grow the same crop or need the same service, live close enough to meet, and trust each other. Agree a clear purpose, such as "sell our maize together and buy inputs in bulk". Hold a first meeting, write minutes, and choose an interim committee.
By-laws are the group's written rules. They usually cover: name, address and purpose; who can join and how; entry fees and shares; meetings, quorum and voting (cooperatives use one member, one vote); the committee, its powers and terms of office; how money is kept and checked; how any surplus is shared; and how members who break rules are disciplined. Your cooperative office often has model by-laws you can adapt.
Registration gives a group legal status to own property, open a bank account in its own name, sign contracts and borrow. Rules differ by country. In Kenya, societies register under the Co-operative Societies Act through the Commissioner for Co-operative Development, starting at the county cooperative office. In Nigeria, the Co-operative Societies Act says a primary society needs at least ten qualified members and applies, with its bye-laws, to the State Director of Co-operatives. In Ghana, groups register with the Department of Co-operatives through its district office. Fees, forms and steps change, so visit or call the office before you apply.
Step by step:
- Agree the group's purpose in one sentence.
- Hold a first meeting; write minutes and members' names.
- Choose an interim committee: chair, secretary, treasurer.
- Get model by-laws from your cooperative office and adapt them.
- Agree the key rules in a members' meeting and record the vote.
- Visit the cooperative office: ask for the current forms, fees and steps.
Words to know:
- By-laws: the written rules a group agrees to follow.
- Quorum: the smallest number of members who must be present for a meeting's decisions to count.
- One member, one vote: each member has one vote, however many shares they hold.
- Registration: official recognition that gives the group legal status.
Official sources:
- Kenya Law: Co-operative Societies Act (registration through the Commissioner for Co-operative Development)
- Nigerian Co-operative Societies Act (Federal and State Directors of Co-operatives; bye-laws; annual audit)
- Ghana Information Services Department: Government begins reform of cooperative sector (Department of Co-operatives)
Try it now: Write five by-law rules for your group: who can join, the entry fee or share, how often you meet and the quorum, how votes work, and what happens if a member side-sells. Then find the address or phone number of your nearest cooperative office.
You can now draft the main by-law rules for a farmer group and know where to register it in your country.

check.q: What does registration give a farmer group?
options: Legal status to own property, open a bank account, sign contracts and borrow
check.why: Registration gives the group legal status to own property, bank, sign contracts and borrow.

check.q: Your group is writing by-laws and does not know where to start. What do you do?
options: Copy a company's rules from the internet
Ask the cooperative office for model by-laws to adapt
Let the chairperson write them alone
check.why: Cooperative offices often have model by-laws that groups can adapt.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Running the group: meetings and records
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Run a short meeting with an agenda and minutes, and set up the group's basic records.
This lesson builds toward: For a group meeting and its money, you will run a meeting with an agenda and minutes, and set up the basic group records, with a member register, cash book, delivery book and payments record, and two people approving payments.
Good meetings build trust. Send the date and agenda ahead (an SMS or WhatsApp message works), start on time, check the quorum, follow the agenda, let every member speak, vote on decisions, and write minutes: who came, what was decided, and who will do what by when. Read the last minutes at the start of each meeting. Hold an annual general meeting where members hear the accounts and elect the committee.
Records are the group's memory and its proof to buyers, banks and the cooperative office. Keep at least: a member register (names, contacts, shares paid), a cash book of all money in and out with receipts, a delivery book showing what each member delivered, its grade and weight, and a payments record showing what each member was paid. Nigeria's Co-operative Societies Act, for example, requires a registered society's accounts to be audited each year.
Protect the money: use a group bank or mobile money account, have two people sign or approve every payment, give receipts for every shilling, naira or cedi, and read the accounts aloud at meetings. A spreadsheet on a phone or a free app can hold records, but keep a paper copy too, and never share PINs or passwords.
Step by step:
- Send the date and agenda ahead.
- Check the quorum; follow the agenda; vote on decisions.
- Write minutes: who came, what was decided, who does what by when.
- Set up four records: members, cash book, deliveries, payments.
- Use a group account with two signatories; give receipts.
- Read the accounts aloud at each meeting; audit once a year.
Words to know:
- Agenda: the list of topics for a meeting.
- Minutes: the written record of what a meeting decided.
- Annual general meeting (AGM): the yearly meeting of all members to hear accounts and elect leaders.
- Audit: an independent check of the group's accounts.
- Signatory: a person allowed to approve payments from an account.
Official sources:
- Nigerian Co-operative Societies Act (Federal and State Directors of Co-operatives; bye-laws; annual audit)
Try it now: Write an agenda for your group's next meeting with four items. Then draw the columns for a delivery book: date, member name, crop, grade, weight, received by.
You can now run a group meeting with an agenda and minutes and keep the records that build trust.

check.q: What happens at an annual general meeting?
options: Members hear the accounts and elect the committee
check.why: At the AGM, members hear the accounts and elect the committee.

check.q: You are chairing today's meeting and the quorum is present. What do you do first?
check.why: Reading the last minutes at the start keeps everyone on track and builds trust.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Aggregation and selling together
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set up a collection day where members' produce is checked, weighed, recorded and paid fairly.
This lesson builds toward: On a collection day, you will check, grade, weigh, record and pay for each member's produce, weighing in front of the member, giving a receipt and paying by the records.
Aggregation means collecting many members' small amounts into one large, even lot. Big buyers such as processors, millers, schools, supermarkets and exporters want steady volumes of one quality, delivered on time. A group that can fill a lorry with clean, dry, graded produce can sell to them and earn more than at the farm gate.
Run a collection point or day with clear rules: the quality the buyer wants (for example dry, clean, sorted maize at the buyer's maximum moisture), a trusted scale, and a record for every delivery. Check and grade each member's produce, weigh it in front of them, write it in the delivery book and give a receipt. Store the lot safely until the buyer collects.
Pay members by the records: weight times the agreed price for their grade, minus any agreed group fee for transport, storage or bags, all decided in advance and written in the by-laws or minutes. Pay on time, through mobile money or the bank where possible. Fast, fair, open payment is the best defence against side-selling.
Step by step:
- Agree the buyer's quality rules and tell all members in advance.
- Set the collection day, place and a trusted scale.
- Check, grade and weigh each delivery in front of the member.
- Write it in the delivery book; give a receipt.
- Store the lot safely; deliver to the buyer together.
- Pay each member by the records, minus agreed fees, on time.
Words to know:
- Aggregation: collecting many small amounts into one large lot.
- Collection point: a place where members bring produce to be checked and recorded.
- Lot: one batch of produce of the same type and grade.
Try it now: Plan one collection day for your group: date, place, scale, the buyer's quality rules, who records, and the group fee per bag or kilo agreed in advance. Write how and when members will be paid.
You can now run a fair collection day and pay members by clear records.

check.q: What is a collection point or day?
options: A place and day where members bring produce to be checked, weighed and recorded
check.why: At a collection point, produce is checked, graded, weighed, recorded and stored until the buyer collects.

check.q: A member's maize is wetter than the buyer allows. What do you do at the collection point?
options: Mix it with dry maize so nobody notices
Do not add it to the lot until it is dried to the buyer's standard
Hide it at the bottom of the lorry
check.why: The lot must meet the buyer's quality, so produce is checked and graded before it is accepted.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Checking market prices by phone
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find prices from at least three sources and work out what an offer is really worth at your farm.
This lesson builds toward: Before selling, you will compare prices from at least three sources and calculate an offer's price at your farm, subtracting transport, fees and losses, and spotting scam offers.
Never sell without knowing the price. Ask at least three buyers, listen to market reports on radio, and check official market information services. In Kenya, the Ministry of Agriculture's KAMIS system publishes wholesale, retail and farm-gate prices for many crops and livestock from markets across the counties. In Nigeria and Ghana, ask your extension office, commodity association or cooperative union which price service covers your crop.
Compare like with like: price per kilo or per bag of the same grade, at the same place. A higher price at a far market may be worth less after transport, loading, market fees and losses. Work out the price at your farm: market price minus all costs of getting it there.
A phone helps. Keep a simple price log each week, share it in the group's WhatsApp, and use a calculator or an AI assistant to compare offers. Be careful of scams: anyone who asks you to pay a fee to receive a "guaranteed" high price, or asks for your mobile money PIN, is not a real buyer.
Step by step:
- Get prices from at least three sources: buyers, radio, official service.
- Check each is for the same crop, grade and unit.
- Subtract transport, loading, fees and losses to get the farm price.
- Log prices weekly and share with the group.
- Ignore anyone asking for a fee or a PIN to get you a price.
Words to know:
- Farm-gate price: the price a buyer pays you at your farm.
- Wholesale price: the price for large amounts sold to traders or shops.
- Market information service: a service that publishes current market prices.
Official sources:
- Kenya Agricultural Market Information System (KAMIS), Ministry of Agriculture
Try it now: This week, get the price for one crop from three sources and write them in a table: source, price, grade, unit, place. Work out the price at your farm for the best two after transport costs. Which offer really pays more?
You can now check prices from several sources and work out which offer really pays more.

check.q: What does "compare like with like" mean for prices?
options: Compare price per kilo or bag of the same grade at the same place
Compare this year with ten years ago
check.why: Prices only compare fairly for the same grade, unit and place.

check.q: Your group wants to follow prices every week. What do you do?
options: Ask one trader once a season
Keep a simple weekly price log and share it in the group's WhatsApp
Wait for the buyer to tell you
check.why: A weekly price log shared in the group helps members know the price before they sell.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Contracts with buyers
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Read a buyer contract and check the key terms before the group signs.
This lesson builds toward: Given a buyer contract, you will check the key terms before the group signs, covering product, grade, quantity, price, delivery, quality checks, payment, failure and disputes.
A contract is a written agreement between the group and a buyer. A good contract gives a sure market and a known price; a bad one can leave the group with produce nobody collects, or money that never comes. Get every deal in writing, even with a buyer you know.
Check these terms: what product and grade; how much and when; the price, or exactly how it will be set (for example the market price on delivery day plus or minus an amount); where delivery happens and who pays transport; how quality is checked and what happens to rejected produce; when and how payment is made; what happens if the harvest fails or the buyer does not collect; and how disputes are settled.
If any part is unclear, ask the buyer to explain in writing. Read it aloud in a members' meeting so everyone understands their duties, including no side-selling. Ask your cooperative office, extension officer or a lawyer to check big contracts. An AI assistant can explain hard words in simple language, but never type the group's bank details or PINs into it, and it does not replace legal advice.
Step by step:
- Get the offer in writing.
- Check product, grade, quantity and dates.
- Check price or how it is set, delivery place and who pays transport.
- Check quality checks, rejection rules, payment date and method.
- Check what happens if the harvest fails or the buyer does not collect, and how disputes are settled.
- Read it to members; have big contracts checked before signing.
Words to know:
- Contract: a written agreement that both sides must keep.
- Rejection: when a buyer refuses produce that does not meet the agreed quality.
- Dispute: a disagreement between the group and the buyer.
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page group selling plan for one crop. Include the group's purpose, five by-law rules, where you would register, your records, how members deliver and are paid, prices from three sources, and the contract terms you will check before signing.
You can now read a buyer contract, check its key terms, and plan how your group will sell together.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Purpose and by-laws No clear purpose, or fewer than five rules. The group's name, purpose and five key by-law rules, such as membership, voting, money and discipline. Rules also cover side-selling and how any surplus is shared. Registration No registration office named. Names the office where the group would register and what must be checked there. Has called or visited the office and noted the current steps and date. Records and money Records missing, or one person controls the money. Member register, cash book, delivery book and payments record, with two people approving payments. Says how accounts will be read to members and checked each year. Delivery, grading and payment No collection or payment rules. How members deliver, how produce is graded and weighed in front of them, and how and when they are paid. Agreed group fees and payment dates are written down in advance. Prices Fewer than three price sources, or no farm-price calculation. Prices from at least three sources, compared like with like, with the price at the farm worked out. Includes a weekly price log over several weeks. Contract terms Fewer than six terms, or key terms such as payment missing. Six contract terms to check, including price, quality, delivery, payment and failure to collect. Names who will check big contracts, such as the cooperative office or a lawyer. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part of the plan and check it again.

options: A written agreement between the group and a buyer
check.why: A contract is a written agreement that sets out what both sides will do.

check.q: Members do not understand the contract's quality terms. What do you do before signing?
options: Sign quickly before the buyer leaves
Ask the buyer to explain in writing and read it aloud at a members' meeting
check.why: Unclear parts are explained in writing and read aloud so every member understands their duties.
